verse.meaning: Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna agrees. The mind is restless, stormy, and stubborn. But it can be trained. The way to train it is through practice and letting go. You do not have to force it still all at once.
verse.for_you: Your mind keeps racing through every possible outcome. That storm is real. But the texts say it can be trained. It does not need to be conquered in one night. It needs practice and letting go. Trust the practice.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment when the mind races, and let it go without fixing it.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna on the five causes behind every action.
verse.sanskrit: अधिष्ठानं तथा कर्ता करणं च पृथग्विधम् । विविधाश्च पृथक्चेष्टा दैवं चैवात्र पञ्चमम् ॥
verse.line: Every result has five causes: the setting, the doer, the tools, the efforts, and the unseen. You're one of them.
verse.translation: The seat, the doer, the various instruments, the many kinds of effort, and fifth, providence: these are the five causes of every action.
verse.why: You are one cause among five; own your part, not the whole outcome.
verse.misuse: Not 'it wasn't my fault'. You own your part; you just aren't the only cause.

prasang.title: What makes an action happen
prasang.summary: Every action has five causes: the setting, the doer, the instruments, the efforts, and providence. Seeing oneself as the only doer is a mistake.
prasang.lesson: You are one cause among five; own your part, not the whole outcome.

verse.meaning: Krishna tells Arjuna that no result happens from a single source. They are listing the five causes that must come together for any action to take place. The setting, the person who acts, the tools they use, the effort they put in, and the unseen force that allows it all to meet. The verse says you are one of these causes. It proposes that you own your part in the action, but you are not the whole outcome. You are one thread in a weave, not the entire cloth.
verse.for_you: You are trying to carry the whole outcome of your work in your own two hands. You are one cause among five, and that means you own your effort but not the final result. The rest belongs to the setting, the tools, the other people, and the unseen.
verse.try_today: Notice the five causes at work in one task today.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own action, one cause among five.
asks: Which of the five causes do I keep forgetting?
How do I know my part is done?

prasang.title: The calm of the wise
prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.
prasang.lesson: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

verse.speaker: Ribhu
verse.setting: Ribhu on inner stillness in an active life.
verse.sanskrit: बहिःकृत्रिमसंरंभो हृदि संरम्भवर्जितः । कर्ता बहिरकर्तान्तर्लोके विहर शुद्धधीः ॥
verse.line: Be busy on the outside and unhurried inside. Act fully, but don't let it agitate you.
verse.translation: Outwardly busy, inwardly free of agitation; a doer on the outside, a non-doer within: move through the world with a clear mind.
verse.why: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

prasang.title: How a free person lives
prasang.summary: Ribhu describes how a free person lives among others: letting go of what is lost, taking up what comes, doing the work at hand, speaking gently, busy outside and calm inside, and treating the whole world as family.
prasang.lesson: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

verse.meaning: Ribhu tells Nidagha that a free person moves through the world with a clear mind. They are busy on the outside and unhurried inside. They act fully, but they do not let the work agitate them. They let go of what is lost and take up what comes. They do the work at hand and speak gently. They treat the whole world as family. The teaching is to live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.
verse.for_you: You are working and your mind is loud with how things will turn out. Ribhu's teaching is that you can be busy on the outside and unhurried inside. The work is yours to do, but the result is not yours to hold.
verse.try_today: Notice the moment your mind starts racing about the result, and let it be.
verse.scene_line: You are busy on the outside and unhurried inside.
asks: How do I let the work be the work?
How do I stop the mind from racing?

verse.speaker: Seer
verse.setting: Follows the call to enjoy by letting go: how to live and work.
verse.sanskrit: कुर्वन्नेवेह कर्माणि जिजीविषेच्छतꣳ समाः । एवं त्वयि नान्यथेतोऽस्ति न कर्म लिप्यते नरे ॥
verse.line: Do your work and wish to live a full hundred years. Done in this spirit, action does not cling.
verse.translation: Doing your work here, you may wish to live a hundred years. For you there is no other way than this: done in this spirit, action does not cling to a person.
verse.why: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

prasang.title: The Isha: enjoy by letting go
prasang.summary: Eighteen verses that open by saying everything belongs to the divine, so we should enjoy it without grasping. They go on to say we should work a full life without being bound, and see ourselves in all beings.
prasang.lesson: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

verse.meaning: The Seer speaks to the reader about the way to live and work. They say you could do your work here, wishing to live a full hundred years. The point is that there is no other way to live than to do your work in this spirit. When you act this way, your actions do not cling to you, and you do not cling to the results.
verse.for_you: You are in that space where the mind will not settle because you are holding on to how it turns out. Your work is yours to do, and the results are not yours to hold. Let that truth steady your hand.
verse.try_today: Work fully today without asking for the result to be a certain way.
verse.scene_line: You are at the kitchen table, the work is laid out, and the hundred years are ahead.
asks: How do I stop the work from clinging to me?
Can I wish for a hundred years without holding on?

story.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
story.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
story.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

anchor.speaker: Janaka
anchor.setting: King Janaka, alone on his palace roof after overhearing wandering sages, rethinks his life.
anchor.sanskrit: संपदश्च विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेच्चित्तेन संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा हन्त मन्ये महापदः ॥ आपदोऽपि विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेन्मनसि संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा मन्ये मनसि संपदः ॥
anchor.line: Good fortune the mind clutches becomes trouble. Trouble the mind accepts becomes a kind of fortune.
anchor.translation: All those dazzling fortunes, if the mind clings to them, are really great calamities in grand disguise. And all those varied misfortunes, if the mind accepts them, are really fortunes.
anchor.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.
anchor.misuse: Accepting a hardship doesn't mean not fixing what can be fixed.
